nodes.title: Thermodynamic Systems & Zeroth Law
points: System: specific region of space under study. Surroundings: everything outside the system boundary.
Open system exchanges both energy and matter; Closed system exchanges energy only; Isolated system exchanges neither.
State variables: Intensive (independent of size, e.g., P, T, density) vs Extensive (dependent on size, e.g., V, U, mass).
Thermodynamic equilibrium requires mechanical (P balanced), chemical (composition constant), and thermal (T uniform) equilibrium.
Zeroth Law of Thermodynamics: If systems A and B are each in thermal equilibrium with system C, then A and B are in thermal equilibrium with each other. This defines Temperature.

formulas.label: Zeroth Law statement
formulas.expr: If T_A = T_C and T_B = T_C ⟹ T_A = T_B

nodes.title: First Law of Thermodynamics & Work Done
points: First Law of Thermodynamics: Conservation of energy for thermodynamic systems: ΔQ = ΔU + W.
Sign conventions (Board standard): Heat added to system ΔQ > 0; heat removed ΔQ < 0.
Work done BY system (expansion) W > 0; work done ON system (compression) W < 0.
Work done in volume change: W = ∫ P dV = area under P–V diagram.
Internal energy U is a state function (depends only on initial and final states, not path). For an ideal gas: ΔU = n C_v ΔT.

nodes.title: Isothermal Process (T = Constant)
points: Temperature remains constant (T = constant, ΔT = 0 ⟹ ΔU = 0).
Follows Boyle's law: PV = constant ⟹ P₁V₁ = P₂V₂.
Conducted very slowly in a container with perfectly conducting walls.
From First Law: Q = W (all absorbed heat is converted into work).
Work done in isothermal expansion: W = nRT ln(V₂/V₁) = 2.303 nRT log₁₀(V₂/V₁) = 2.303 nRT log₁₀(P₁/P₂).
Slope of isothermal curve on P–V diagram: dP/dV = −P/V.

nodes.title: Adiabatic Process (Q = 0)
points: No heat exchange with surroundings (Q = 0, insulated walls, sudden/rapid process).
Follows Poisson's relations: PV^γ = constant, T V^(γ−1) = constant, P^(1−γ) T^γ = constant.
From First Law: ΔU = −W. If system expands (W > 0), ΔU < 0 (gas cools); if compressed (W < 0), gas heats up.
Work done in adiabatic process: W = (P₁V₁ − P₂V₂) / (γ − 1) = nR(T₁ − T₂) / (γ − 1).
Slope of adiabatic curve: dP/dV = −γ(P/V). Adiabatic curve is γ times steeper than isothermal curve.

nodes.title: Isobaric, Isochoric & Cyclic Processes
points: Isobaric process (P = constant): W = P(V₂ − V₁) = nR(T₂ − T₁). Q = n C_p ΔT; ΔU = n C_v ΔT.
Isochoric process (V = constant): dV = 0 ⟹ W = 0. All heat changes internal energy: Q = ΔU = n C_v ΔT.
Cyclic process: System returns to initial state. ΔU = 0 for a complete cycle. Net work W_net = Q_net = area enclosed by P–V loop.
Clockwise P–V loop represents positive work done by system (heat engine); anticlockwise loop represents work done on system (refrigerator).

formulas.label: Isochoric work
formulas.expr: W = 0 , Q = ΔU = n C_v ΔT

nodes.title: Heat Engines & Second Law of Thermodynamics
points: Heat engine converts thermal energy into mechanical work through a cyclic process.
Essential parts: Source at high temp T_H, working substance, and Sink at lower temp T_C.
Efficiency: η = W / Q_H = (Q_H − Q_C) / Q_H = 1 − Q_C / Q_H.

Kelvin-Planck statement: It is impossible to construct an engine operating in a cycle that absorbs heat from a reservoir and converts it completely into work without rejecting heat (η cannot be 100%).
Clausius statement: It is impossible for heat to flow spontaneously from a colder body to a hotter body without external work.

nodes.title: Carnot Cycle & Ideal Engine Efficiency
points: Carnot engine is an ideal, reversible heat engine operating between two temperatures T_H and T_C.
Four reversible stages: (1) Isothermal expansion at T_H, (2) Adiabatic expansion from T_H to T_C, (3) Isothermal compression at T_C, (4) Adiabatic compression from T_C to T_H.
Efficiency of Carnot engine: η_carnot = 1 − T_C / T_H (depends only on operating temperatures in Kelvin).
Carnot's theorem: No real engine operating between two given temperatures can be more efficient than a Carnot engine operating between the same temperatures.
To achieve 100% efficiency, sink temp T_C must be 0 K or source temp T_H must be ∞, which are practically impossible.

nodes.title: Refrigerators, Heat Pumps & COP
points: A refrigerator is a heat engine working in reverse: absorbs heat Q_C from cold reservoir, external work W is done on it, rejects heat Q_H to hot reservoir.
Coefficient of Performance (COP) of refrigerator: α = Q_C / W = Q_C / (Q_H − Q_C).
For ideal Carnot refrigerator: α_carnot = T_C / (T_H − T_C).
Heat pump extracts heat from cold surroundings to warm an interior space: COP_HP = Q_H / W = T_H / (T_H − T_C).
Fundamental link between Heat Pump and Refrigerator COP: COP_HP = α + 1.

nodes.title: Must-Know Board Derivations & Diagrams
points: Board Favourite #1: Derive work done during isothermal expansion: W = 2.303 nRT log₁₀(V₂/V₁).
Board Favourite #2: Derive work done during adiabatic expansion: W = nR(T₁ − T₂)/(γ − 1).
Board Favourite #3: Draw and explain the four stages of the Carnot cycle with neat P–V diagram.
Board Favourite #4: State First Law of Thermodynamics and apply it to (a) Isothermal, (b) Adiabatic, (c) Isobaric, (d) Isochoric processes.
Distinctions to Master: Reversible vs Irreversible process; Isothermal vs Adiabatic process.

nodes.title: MHT-CET Shortcuts, PV-Loop Traps & Memory Tricks
points: Slope Comparison: |Slope_adiabatic| = γ × |Slope_isothermal|. Since γ > 1, adiabatic curve is always steeper.
Expansion Work Comparison: For same initial state and same expansion to V₂: W_isobaric > W_isothermal > W_adiabatic.
Compression Work Comparison: For same initial state and compression to V₂: W_adiabatic > W_isothermal > W_isobaric (adiabatic requires maximum work).
Carnot Efficiency Shortcut: η = (T_H − T_C) / T_H. Increasing T_H by ΔT gives less efficiency gain than decreasing T_C by same ΔT.
Cyclic Area Shortcut: Area of elliptical P–V loop = π × a × b = π × (ΔP/2) × (ΔV/2).
Trap: In adiabatic expansion, gas cools (T decreases, ΔU < 0); in adiabatic compression, gas heats up (T increases, ΔU > 0).
